subject: botany
question_text: Give a brief account of the types of chromosomes based on the position of the centromere.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack botany section, Chapter 9 'The Unit of Life' (book pp.23-26), which prints the question and a model answer but NO star rank and NO year citations - so stars are 0 and appearances are empty by fact, not by omission. Only ONE source book is held for botany: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no botany board paper is in the corpus. The two-book union check and the back-test are therefore STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this card, not merely unrun - never read this as 'checked and clean'. The mark split is this card's claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. FIGURE SCOPE: the book's diagram labels Satellite and Secondary constriction as well as the four types. Adding them here would have crowded a four-panel figure past the label-collision limit, so this card's figure shows the four types and their arms, and the satellite gets its own labelled sketch on the VSAQ card ts_ipe_b1_ul_satellite_chromosome.

steps.label: The basis
lines: Every chromosome has a primary constriction
called the centromere, which divides the
chromosome into two arms.
The position of the centromere fixes the
relative length of the two arms, and so the
shape of the chromosome.
On this basis chromosomes are of four types.
steps.why: All four names describe one thing — how far the centromere lies from the end — so the classification only makes sense once the centromere and the arms are defined.
common_mistakes: Writing that the classification is based on chromosome length. It is based on centromere position.
Naming only three types. There are four.
steps.memory_tip: Move the centromere from the middle to the tip and you pass through all four types in order.
steps.margin_note: Define centromere and arms before naming the types.

steps.label: Labelled diagram
steps.why: The four drawings earn the mark only if the arm lengths differ correctly: equal for metacentric, clearly unequal for sub-metacentric, very unequal for acrocentric, and one arm only for telocentric.
common_mistakes: Drawing all four with the centromere in the same place.
Leaving out the short arm and long arm labels.
steps.memory_tip: Draw them in order — middle, off-middle, near the end, at the end.
steps.margin_note: Four small sketches side by side; label one of them fully.

steps.label: Metacentric, sub-metacentric
lines: Metacentric: the centromere lies in the
middle, so the two arms are equal. The
chromosome looks like a 'V' at anaphase.
Sub-metacentric: the centromere lies nearer
one end, giving one shorter arm and one longer
arm, so the chromosome looks like an 'L'.
steps.why: These two differ only in where the centromere sits, so the answer must give the arm lengths for each and not just the name.
common_mistakes: Writing that a sub-metacentric has equal arms.
Writing that a metacentric has a terminal centromere.
steps.memory_tip: Meta = middle, so equal arms. Sub-meta = just off middle, so one arm is shorter.
steps.margin_note: Give arm lengths for each type, not just the name.

steps.label: Acrocentric, telocentric

lines.text: Meta → sub-meta → acro → telo: centromere moves out

lines: Acrocentric: the centromere lies close to one
end, giving one very short arm and one very
long arm. A satellite is often carried on the
short arm.
Telocentric: the centromere is terminal, at one
tip, so the chromosome has a single arm and
looks like a rod.
steps.why: Acro means at the tip and telo means the end itself, so an acrocentric still keeps a short arm while a telocentric has none at all.
common_mistakes: Treating acrocentric and telocentric as the same. An acrocentric still has a short arm.
Writing that a telocentric has two arms.
steps.memory_tip: Acro = almost at the end, so a stub is left. Telo = at the end, so no stub.
steps.margin_note: The acro-versus-telo difference is the mark students lose.

insider_note: The book's own diagram also carries a satellite and a secondary constriction — add the satellite on the acrocentric's short arm if there is room.
